title: Isidasi's story
hook: three husbands sent her back; she tells the long tale behind it (Therigatha, Isidasi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punnika asked a shivering brahmin why he bathed. Your line was the frogs would be saints. Did you ask, kindly, what one habit was really for? Today, a nun who is asked why, and answers at length. Day seven hundred ninety-four.

Two nuns sit together after the alms round, in the city of Pataliputta. One of them, Bodhi, asks the other a question that's half compliment and half puzzle. You're still young, and lovely, she says. What did you see that made you leave the world? The other nun is Isidasi. She doesn't answer with a slogan. She tells the whole story, and it's long, and it doesn't flatter anyone, not even herself. Today's lesson is a woman who was asked why, and told everything.
screen: `TWO NUNS AFTER THE ALMS ROUND.` → `WHY DID YOU LEAVE THE WORLD?` → `SHE TELLS EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: First, the faithful wife. Isidasi says she was married into a merchant family in Saketa, and she did all a daughter-in-law was expected to do. She bowed to her in-laws morning and evening, cooked, cleaned, served her husband with her own hands. And still he came to hate her. When his parents asked what she had done, she told them: nothing. I've done no wrong. They sent her home to her father. Second, again and again. Her father gave her to a second husband, who sent her back too. Then her father invited a wandering beggar to stay as his son-in-law. Before long the man asked for his begging bowl and robe back, and left. Three times, and no one could name a fault. So, with her father's blessing, she went forth. Third, the longer story. Here the poem turns. Isidasi says she can now see her past lives, and she tells them: once a goldsmith who went after other men's wives, then long suffering, then births as animals, then hard human lives. In her telling, being sent away in this life was that old deed ripening. Fourth, how to hear it. Some readers find this ending hard, because it can sound like blaming a woman for being rejected. But notice what the poem insists on first: in this life she did nothing wrong. Her husbands couldn't name a fault, and neither could she. The past-life story is her searching out the whole shape of what happened, further back than one life, and then setting it down. She ends the poem free of all of it.
screen: `A FAITHFUL WIFE, SENT HOME.` · `TWICE MORE, AND NO FAULT FOUND.` · `A GOLDSMITH, LIVES AGO.` · `BLAMELESS NOW, AND FREE AT LAST.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to listen to someone's whole story. Bring to mind a person whose life you know only by its headline: the divorce, the move, the illness, the job that ended. Settle. Picture asking them, the way Bodhi asked Isidasi, how did it happen? Then picture not interrupting. Not fixing. Letting the story be as long as it is. Breathe into that patience now, so it's ready when the moment comes. The bell holds the time.
Isidasi's story. Asked why she left the world, a nun told all of it: marriages that failed through no fault she could find, and a past that reached back through other lives. Today's word.
Your line: the whole story. Today, when someone tells you what happened, ask one more question before you decide what you think. Day seven hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Isidasi's poem is read in Buddhist communities as a teaching on kamma across lives, and modern readers also discuss it as an account of a woman's marriages told in her own voice.

fork.setup: you're Isidasi's father. your daughter has been sent back twice, and no one can say why. what do you do?
options: keep her at home and stop trying.
invite a wandering beggar to stay as her husband.
send her straight to the nuns.
fork.reveal: he invites a beggar to be his son-in-law. before long the man asks for his bowl and robe and goes. only then does Isidasi go forth, with her father's blessing.

original.note: Pali kamma (Sanskrit karma): deed, action. Isidasi traces this life's sorrow to a deed lives ago.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sad tale of a rejected wife.
what it means: asked why she left the world, Isidasi tells the whole of it: blameless in this life, sent away three times, and an old deed reaching back through other lives.
what a scholar hears: the poem is framed as a dialogue, Bodhi's question and Isidasi's answer, and its past-life section traces kamma through a chain of births, ending in her freedom from it.

notes: All text is paraphrased; no translation quoted.

Sensitive: the poem explains her rejection as the ripening of past-life deeds. The script stresses that the poem calls her blameless in this life and offers 'some readers find this hard' without ranking; Keeper should confirm the framing is faithful to the tradition's reading of kamma.

Confirm the paraphrase of Thig 15.1: Bodhi's question in Pataliputta; marriage into a merchant family of Saketa; her service to in-laws and husband; her answer that she had done no wrong; the second husband; the mendicant who asked for his bowl and robe back; going forth with her father's permission (the commentary names the nun Jinadatta, left out); past lives as a goldsmith committing adultery, then hell, animal births and hard human births.
The index says three husbands; the script counts the three marriages the poem itself tells.
